note: Written cold from decomposePrompt without sight of the validator — the closest thing here to real model output. Negotiation turned the unscopeable "AI" into a bounded goal in two turns.

goal.statement: Trace a single token through a small transformer and say what each stage does to it, and why attention is the part that makes it work.
goal.audience: a programmer with no machine learning background

capstone.prompt: Take the sentence "the cat sat on the" and walk through what happens to the word "cat" from input to the model's prediction of the next word. Say what attention contributes that a plain feed-forward network could not.
rubric: follows the token as a vector through each stage
explains attention as weighted mixing of other positions
names what is learned versus what is computed
does not treat the model as a lookup table

assumed: what an array of numbers is

kcs.label: A token is a chunk of text — often a word-piece — mapped to an integer id
misconceptions: a token is always a whole word
tokens are individual characters

check.stem: How is "unbelievable" most likely handled by a tokenizer?
options: split into a few word-pieces, each with its own id
kept as one whole word with one id
split into individual letters
looked up in a dictionary of English words
distractorSource: a token is always a whole word
tokens are individual characters
a token is always a whole word

kcs.label: An embedding turns a token id into a vector of numbers
misconceptions: the vector stores the word's letters
the embedding is looked up from a fixed dictionary rather than learned

check.stem: What does the embedding layer produce for a token id?
options: a vector of numbers, learned during training
the word's letters encoded as numbers
a fixed vector from a standard published dictionary
a single number ranking the word's frequency
distractorSource: the vector stores the word's letters
the embedding is looked up from a fixed dictionary rather than learned
the vector stores the word's letters

kcs.label: Vectors sit in a learned space where nearby means used alike
misconceptions: the dimensions have human-readable meanings
the space was designed by hand rather than learned from data

check.stem: "King" and "queen" end up close together because…
options: they are used in similar contexts
one dimension literally encodes royalty
someone chose to place related words near each other
one dimension encodes gender and another rank
distractorSource: the dimensions have human-readable meanings
the space was designed by hand rather than learned from data
the dimensions have human-readable meanings

kcs.label: Attention has no sense of order, so position must be written into the vector
misconceptions: the model reads left to right like a person
order is preserved automatically because the input is a list

check.stem: Why must position be added to the vectors at all?
options: attention alone would treat a shuffled sentence identically
the model would otherwise read the sentence backwards
it makes the model faster
it stops words repeating
distractorSource: the model reads left to right like a person
order is preserved automatically because the input is a list
order is preserved automatically because the input is a list

kcs.label: Each position turns its vector into a query, a key and a value
misconceptions: query, key and value are three different words' vectors
they are stored lookups rather than computed each time

check.stem: Where do a position's query, key and value come from?
options: all three are computed from that position's own vector
from three neighbouring words
from a table stored during training
the query is the word, the key is the sentence
distractorSource: query, key and value are three different words' vectors
they are stored lookups rather than computed each time
query, key and value are three different words' vectors

kcs.label: Every query is scored against every key, and the scores become weights summing to one
misconceptions: only the highest-scoring position is used
the scores are the final output rather than weights

check.stem: After scoring, what happens to the scores?
options: they are turned into weights across all positions that add to one
the single best position is picked and the rest discarded
they are passed on as the layer's output
they are averaged into one number
distractorSource: only the highest-scoring position is used
the scores are the final output rather than weights
only the highest-scoring position is used

kcs.label: A position's output is the weighted sum of every position's value
misconceptions: the position copies the winning word's vector
the output replaces information from other positions rather than blending it

check.stem: What does a position hold after one attention step?
options: a blend of all positions' values, weighted by relevance
a copy of the most relevant word's vector
its own vector, unchanged
the average of every word in the sentence
distractorSource: the position copies the winning word's vector
the output replaces information from other positions rather than blending it
the position copies the winning word's vector

kcs.label: The per-position MLP transforms each vector alone, mixing nothing between positions
misconceptions: the MLP also lets positions see each other
the MLP is where the sentence is understood

check.stem: What can the per-position MLP see?
options: only its own position's vector
every position in the sentence
the two neighbouring positions
the original text
distractorSource: the MLP also lets positions see each other
the MLP also lets positions see each other
the MLP is where the sentence is understood

kcs.label: Attention is the only place one position reads another — that is what a plain feed-forward net cannot do
misconceptions: a deep enough feed-forward network could do the same
attention is mainly a speed optimisation

check.stem: Why can't a stack of per-position MLPs replace attention?
options: no position could ever read another's content
it would be too slow to train
it would use more memory
it could, with enough layers
distractorSource: attention is mainly a speed optimisation
attention is mainly a speed optimisation
a deep enough feed-forward network could do the same

kcs.label: Each block adds its result back onto the vector instead of replacing it
misconceptions: each layer overwrites the previous one's output
the residual connection is only a training trick with no effect on meaning

check.stem: What happens to a position's vector as it passes through a block?
options: the block's output is added to what was already there
it is replaced by the block's output
it is reset before each block
it is averaged with the block's output
distractorSource: each layer overwrites the previous one's output
each layer overwrites the previous one's output
the residual connection is only a training trick with no effect on meaning

kcs.label: Blocks stack, so a late layer reads a vector many earlier blocks have written to
misconceptions: each layer starts fresh from the embedding
later layers see only the layer immediately before

options: the accumulated vector every earlier block has added to
only layer 19's output
the original embedding again
the raw token id
distractorSource: later layers see only the layer immediately before
each layer starts fresh from the embedding
each layer starts fresh from the embedding

kcs.label: The final vector is scored against every word in the vocabulary to pick the next one
misconceptions: the model outputs a word directly
it retrieves a stored continuation it saw in training

check.stem: What does the model actually output at the end?
options: a score for every word in the vocabulary
the next word as text
a sentence it memorised
the vector itself
distractorSource: the model outputs a word directly
it retrieves a stored continuation it saw in training
the model outputs a word directly

kcs.label: Weights are learned once and fixed; the vectors are computed fresh for every input
misconceptions: the model learns while you talk to it
the activations are stored somewhere between requests

check.stem: You send the same prompt twice. What is reused?
options: the weights; the vectors are recomputed from scratch
both weights and vectors, from a cache
nothing — it relearns each time
the vectors; the weights are recomputed
distractorSource: the activations are stored somewhere between requests
the model learns while you talk to it
the model learns while you talk to it
